newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Afghan factions hold second day of peace talks.
newsitem.headline: Afghan factions hold second day of peace talks.

text.p: Warring Afghan factions held a second day of peace talks in Islamabad on Tuesday, while Pakistan's foreign minister flew to Tehran to try to coordinate policy towards Afghanistan with Iranian leaders.
"We had a very good session today," a U.N. official said. "There was a vigorous, but friendly and constructive, exchange of views...and we are continuing tomorrow."
He would not disclose if the three representatives of the Taleban Islamic movement had reached any specific agreement yet with their three counterparts from an opposition alliance.

The talks were in full swing when Pakistani Foreign Minister Sahibzada Yaqoob Khan left to meet his Iranian opposite number Ali Akbar Velayati for talks in which Afghanistan was expected to top the agenda, the official news agency APP reported.
It said Khan was also expected to meet Iranian President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani during his three-day stay in Tehran.
Iran and Pakistan hold contrasting views of the Taleban, viewed with deep suspicion in Tehran, but have sought to contain their differences by maintaining a dialogue on Afghanistan.
Both countries say they support U.N. peace efforts and deny favouring any one Afghan faction over another.
The U.N.-sponsored Afghan peace talks, which began on Monday, have much ground to cover if they are to reconcile the deep divisions between the two sides.
The purist Islamic Taleban demand that a ceasefire be established and an exchange of prisoners take place before any further discussions on the future of Afghanistan.
The opposition has demanded that Kabul, which fell to the Taleban on September 27, be demilitarised and handed over to a neutral security force as part of any ceasefire deal.
The Taleban have rejected the idea of demilitarising Kabul, where tanks often rumble through the war-shattered streets and Taleban fighters race round the city in battered pick-up trucks.

Previous attempts by the United Nations to broker peace in Afghanistan have ended in failure. In 1995, Holl's predecessor said he had an agreement from then-President Burhanuddin Rabbani to step down in favour of an interim administration.
The deal foundered when the Taleban refused to take part, giving Rabbani a pretext to back out of his commitment.
